analysis.one_liner: Requires passenger-carrying commercial helicopters to carry flight data and cockpit voice recorders.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on February 26, 2020, sent to its Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for an air carrier to fly a turbine-powered helicopter carrying passengers unless it has a flight data recorder and a cockpit voice recorder, the same 'black box' equipment long required on large airplanes. It would take effect one year after enactment. The recorders don't prevent crashes; they capture flight data and cockpit conversation so investigators can determine why a crash happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Helicopter passengers and crews, their families, and accident investigators. When a helicopter crashes, recorded flight data and cockpit audio are often the only way to establish the cause, which is what leads to future safety fixes. Families of victims also gain a factual account instead of an unresolved mystery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Helicopter passengers, crews, and victims' families

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for an air carrier to operate a single- or multiengine, turbine-powered helicopter with one or more passenger seats and one or more pilots unless it carries a flight data recorder and a cockpit voice recorder meeting federal aviation standards (14 CFR 91.609). [S3]
The requirement would take effect one year after enactment, giving operators time to install the equipment. [S3]
Recorders give crash investigators the flight data and cockpit audio needed to determine a crash's cause, which is how aviation safety rules get improved after accidents.

analysis.who_pays: Air carriers that operate passenger helicopters — sightseeing and tour operators, air medical services, and other commercial operators — would bear the cost of buying, installing, and maintaining recorders on aircraft that currently don't have them. Those costs would likely be passed on to customers through higher ticket prices, and some small operators might retire older aircraft rather than retrofit them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Passenger helicopter operators and their customers

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes equipment and maintenance costs on commercial helicopter operators, including small air medical and tour operators, with no federal funding to offset them; some of that cost lands on customers through higher fares.
Recorders are an investigative tool, not a preventive one: the bill would not stop a single crash by itself, only improve the ability to learn from crashes after they happen.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is modest but real and permanent: every future crash of a covered helicopter can be properly investigated, which is how the industry's strong safety record in accidents that get investigated gets built in the first place. The cost is likewise modest — cockpit recorders are mature, widely available technology — but falls entirely on operators without subsidies, and a one-year effective date is tight for retrofitting fleets. A fair reading is that this is a reasonable, low-cost safety measure that simply never got considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee in February 2020, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony G. Brown (D-MD) introduced the bill on February 26, 2020, for himself and Rep. Maxine Waters. [S1]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Aviation Subcommittee. [S5]
Only one member, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), cosponsored the bill. [S4]
No further action was recorded for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021; the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial helicopter operators are better off: because the bill died without consideration, they face no recorder installation mandate or its costs. Passengers on covered helicopter flights gained nothing, since no comparable requirement was enacted in its place.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; no votes were ever taken, so the partisan split on the underlying idea was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Passenger helicopter operators (tour, air medical, and other commercial carriers)
industries.note: The bill would require them to buy, install, and maintain recorders on helicopters that currently fly without them, an unfunded cost that would partly fall on customers. Their interest in avoiding that cost runs against passengers' interest in having crashes fully investigated.

The mandate would create demand for flight data and cockpit voice recorder units for retrofits across the passenger helicopter fleet. Their gain comes with the safety benefit to passengers, so their interest runs alongside the public's.
